assistant.content:
Below is a high-level overview of the most important security features found on modern banknotes (paper‐ or polymer-based) and the rough approaches counterfeiters use to mimic them.  This is meant for educational/detection purposes only—not as a how-to guide.

1. Substrate (Paper vs. Polymer)  
   • Genuine:  
     – Cotton-linen blend (most USD, GBP, etc.) or specially formulated polymer (EUR, AUD, CAD, etc.)  
     – Unique feel (soft, slightly fibrous or smooth plastic-like)  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Off-the-shelf “cotton” or rag papers, heavy linen stationery  
     – Thin plastic films or coated papers to approximate polymer  

2. Watermarks  
   • Genuine:  
     – Embedded into the paper during manufacturing  
     – Visible as a shaded image when held to light  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Light-printing on thinner paper to fake translucency  
     – Digitally printed “watermarks” that lack true depth  

3. Security Thread (Embedded or Windowed)  
   • Genuine:  
     – Metalized or plastic thread woven into or appearing intermittently on the surface  
     – Often microprinted or containing UV-reactive elements  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Thin foil or plastic strips glued on or sandwiched between layers  
     – Simple dark lines printed over the note  

4. Intaglio & Raised Printing  
   • Genuine:  
     – Deep relief printing giving a tactile “ridge” you can feel with your fingernail  
     – Crisp fine lines and sharp edges  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Letterpress, thermographic (“raised varnish”) or spot-UV coatings to simulate texture  
     – Glossy toner build-up from laser printers  

5. Microprinting  
   • Genuine:  
     – Extremely small text (<0.5 mm tall) visible only under magnification  
     – Sharp, continuous strokes  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Regular high-resolution scans/prints that blur or break into dots  
     – Scaled-down fonts not designed for true microprint  

6. Color-Shifting (Optically Variable) Inks & Holograms  
   • Genuine:  
     – Inks that change color at different viewing angles  
     – Multi-layer holographic patches or stripes  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Simple metallic foils or low-grade “iridescent” films  
     – Static two-tone inks that don’t truly shift with angle  

7. UV- and IR-Reactive Features  
   • Genuine:  
     – Patterns, fibers or inks that glow (or disappear) under ultraviolet or infrared light  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Generic fluorescent inks purchased off-the-shelf  
     – Omission of IR marks entirely (many low-end fakes lack any IR response)  

8. Magnetic Inks & Infrared Elements  
   • Genuine:  
     – Special magnetic or IR-absorbing pigments in designated areas  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Rarely reproduced—most fakes fail machine-read checks  

9. See-Through Registers & Latent Images  
   • Genuine:  
     – Tiny elements printed on both sides that align perfectly when backlit  
     – Hidden images visible only at certain angles  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Single-side printing or misaligned double-side prints  
     – Crude simulated shapes that don’t match up exactly  

10. Guilloche Patterns & Fine Line Artwork  
   • Genuine:  
     – Complex, mathematically generated linework extremely difficult to redraw  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Standard raster graphics or low-dpi scans that lose crispness  
     – Simple geometric fills that “give away” a copy  

11. Serial Numbers & Fonts  
   • Genuine:  
     – Unique alphanumeric sequences, consistent font, precise spacing  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Repeated or sequential numbers duplicated across multiple notes  
     – Slightly off fonts or spacing errors  

12. Additional Tactile or Machine-Readable Features  
   • Genuine:  
     – Raised dots/lines for the visually impaired  
     – Embedded RFID tags (very rare) or digital watermarks  
   • Counterfeit approaches:  
     – Often ignored or superficially imitated  

COMMON COUNTERFEITING METHODS (AT A GLANCE)  
 • High-resolution flatbed/sheet‐fed scanning  
 • Commercial offset lithography or plate printing  
 • Home/office laser and inkjet printers  
 • Chemical washing (bleaching) of low‐denomination notes, then re-printing  
 • Foil stamping for hologram/stripe simulacra  
 • Hand‐engraving or photo-etching to produce crude intaglio plates  
 • Application of generic UV/fluorescent inks under clear coatings  

Key takeaway for detection: genuine notes rely on a combination of substrate, tactile feel, micro-precision, and optically variable elements that are very hard to replicate all at once.  Counterfeits typically succeed at imitating only a few features—inspection under magnification, UV/IR light, by touch, and against light will often reveal discrepancies.
